title: Michael Shaulov | The Gatekeeper Unlocking Institutional Access to Crypto | Talks at Google
description:
Fireblocks co-founder and CEO Michael Shaulov meets with CapitalG founder David Lawee to discuss Fireblocks and how the company is well-positioned to win the institutional custody market.

The entrance point for any individual to the world of Web3 is a crypto wallet. For institutions, that first step is custody, which enables the secure storage and transfer of digital assets. Eventually every major institution in the world–from the Fortune 1000 to small businesses and even nonprofits–will interact with Web3. Plug-and-play custody solutions will be their mission-critical gateway to this multi-trillion-dollar market.

Fireblocks has emerged as the winner in the institutional custody market, thanks to their differentiated strategy of being infrastructure-only, security-first, and product-oriented. As a result, Fireblocks has created the industry’s largest over-the-counter crypto settlement network. Through its API-based infrastructure and growing network of trading parties, Fireblocks is strategically placed to expand deeper into DeFi, trade settlement, lending, tokenization and potentially a host of other exciting new digital assets businesses.

Michael Shaulov is the CEO and co-founder of Fireblocks, a secure digital asset infrastructure company. Prior to Fireblocks, he co-founded Lacoon Mobile Security, which was acquired by Check Point, and was then appointed the Head of Products, Mobile and Cloud Security for Check Point. Michael is a serial cybersecurity entrepreneur and investor. He is also a recognized industry speaker, delivering talks at RSA Conference, BlackHat and Infosec. Before his commercial endeavors, Michael pioneered the mobile security field in an elite military technological unit (8200), where he received the Israeli Presidential Excellency Honor for his contributions. He holds a BSc in Computer Sciences and Physics from Ben-Gurion University, Israel.

Moderated by David Lawee.

David Lawee founded CapitalG, Alphabet's independent growth fund, in 20
summary: The speakers discuss the founding of Fireblocks, which was triggered by a 2017 cyber attack on South Korean exchanges that stole $200 million and revealed a gap in secure, scalable digital asset infrastructure. Michael Shaulov and his co-founders built the company to address this need by offering secured digital asset infrastructure that allows customers to custody assets, access DeFi, mint and burn tokens, and manage treasury operations.

transcript: [MUSIC PLAYING] DAVID LAWEE: Hi, welcome, everyone and thanks for joining us today for "Talks at Google". I'm David Lawee, the founder and general partner at Capital G, which is Alphabet's independent growth fund, making investments into late stage technology companies. My team leads the firm's crypto investment strategy. So I'm thrilled to bring in today's guests to discuss Fireblocks, one of the most valuable companies in Web3. Fireblocks has emerged as the winner in institutional custody and more broadly, kind of just a terrific software company recently valued at $8 billion. They offer secured digital asset infrastructure allowing customers to custody assets, access DeFi, mint and burn tokens, and manage their treasury operations. Before we start, I want to remind the audience that we'll be taking live questions. That's the purpose of this interaction, to give people a chance to ask their own questions. As you think of them, please just introduce them into the live chat on the right. And with that, I'm very excited to introduce today's guest, Michael Shaulov. Michael is the CEO and co-founder of Fireblocks. He is a cybersecurity entrepreneur and investor, serial entrepreneur. Prior to co-founding Fireblocks, Michael co-founded Lacoon Mobile Security, which was acquired by Checkpoint. He ran products and mobile Cloud security for Checkpoint. And before his commercial endeavors, Michael pioneered the mobile security field in the elite military technology unit, the 8200, which I'm sure many people have heard of, where he received the Israeli Presidential Excellency Honor for his contributions. He holds a BSC in computer science and physics from Ben Gurion University. Michael, it's my pleasure to welcome you to "Talks at Google". MICHAEL SHAULOV: Thanks for having me. I'm super excited to be on this podcast. DAVID LAWEE: Yeah, you're like a podcast professional. Let's start with the founding story of Fireblocks. I think most people dream about starting a company. You've started multiple companies. Tell us how this one came together. MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, sure. So my previous company, as you mentioned, was acquired by Checkpoint. And I was basically running the mobile and Cloud security products. And what happened in 2017 was that there was basically a cyber attack in South Korea, where four exchanges got hacked over there, presumably by the North Korean, by the Lazarus Group. And they stole about $200 million from those four exchanges. Because Checkpoint's [INAUDIBLE] all business and we developed a lot of the mobile security expertise over there, we were part of the investigation team. And we started to look into that attack. And that was sort of the first time that I sort kind of went down the rabbit hole of crypto by looking at those businesses. And I think the two things we've realized was one, it was a pretty remarkable hack and a pretty remarkable [INAUDIBLE] in terms of the amount of value that they were able to steal in a fairly short period of time. And the second thing that we started to realize is that once you actually start to read about crypto, or more broadly, basically blockchain and digital assets, you sort of understand that this is kind of transformational technology for finance in general, and probably as we actually starting to realize today, probably goes well beyond finance. But I think what was obvious for us in 2017 is that it's going to revolutionize finance. So we started to discuss with the players in the space, that were active in the institutional crypto space back in 2017, early 2018, there weren't a lot of them, clearly not the same amount as we have today. But that's where we sort of recognized that there is a huge gap in terms of what the promise is, what existed in the market for really doing it in a secure and scalable way. And I think this is what sort of triggered us to go and build Fireblocks. DAVID LAWEE: Awesome. But who was in the institutional crypto space at that time? Like what are the types of players? MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, so there were a bunch of exchanges. And they were mostly sort of OTC desk and trading desk. So Coinbase and Binance was there, Bitstamp. There were some of those South Korean crypto exchanges, like [? Upbit ?] and [? QCoin, ?] and a few of those that some of them actually went out of business after that hack. And then you had companies like Genesis, that you guys are sort of also direct investors through DCG. They actually became our first customer after we started the company, and people like Galaxy. So they were mostly on the trading side. I would say that was more or less the space when we started. Clearly there were quite a few of those other names, [INAUDIBLE] and [INAUDIBLE],, and so on. But that's what we started to go after. DAVID LAWEE: And who were your co-founders? Who are your co-founders? MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, so my two co-founders are Idan Ofrat and Pavel. So Pavel is our VP R&D. And Idan is our CTO. They're the folks that I co-founded the company with. They have very background to mine. I actually served with them. We go back about 20 years, served together in the army with Pavel basically in the same section. And Idan was in the computing unit, unit A1. And then Pavel was basically, our VP of research in Lacoon. And after we got acquired by Checkpoint, he basically assumed all the engineering for the mobile products. And Idan had a slightly different career path. But he also basically started as being a VP R&D for a company in the cybersecurity space that got acquired. Then actually he sort of pivoted into the climtech space. He had actually a venture in solar energy. And then he sort of came back full circle to cyber. DAVID LAWEE: And how did you divide up the initial responsibilities? MICHAEL SHAULOV: Well, I think that I already had the experience from the-- I think in our case, it was reasonably easy, at least on my side. I was the CEO of the previous company. So it was almost kind of reasonable that I'll be the CEO here. Pavel had the experience of running a pretty big team of-- sorry. DAVID LAWEE: [INAUDIBLE]. MICHAEL SHAULOV: Thank you. Pretty big team of about, say, 100 or so, 150 engineers back in Checkpoint. And his background was basically being an engineering manager. And Idan definitely was sort of the most robust background of being both a CTO, a chief product officer, and also VP R&D in certain capacities. So he sort of assumed the product, which we have-- because we are a pretty cutting edge technology company, I think in our case, the product and the CTO we view this as sort of one unified executive position. Because the head of pushing the envelope on the innovation and then figuring out how to productize it and essentially, guide the R&D in terms of what they need to build. And eventually Pavel sort makes sure that we build it and deliver it. DAVID LAWEE: And the first solution, what did it solve? And what technology did you leverage? MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, so I think one of the key things that we've learned during this kind of initial market exploration-- so I'm a big believer in the customer discovery process. It actually served me very well in the first startup, in Lacoon. And I was sort of preaching it to all the other ventures that I was involved. And there is a book that I really like called "The Four Steps to Epiphany" that Steve Blank wrote almost 20 years ago. So that's like my Bible. I actually have five copies of this book [INAUDIBLE] my table. And basically everyone who walks into my room, I give them a copy. Maybe I should like ask for some royalties on that. But what happened was that after that hack that I just described, we went to all those players. Before we actually starting Fireblocks, we talked with, I think, 40 or so prospects in the space and sort of try to understand what are their pain points? How do they operate? And just sort of try to almost give free consulting around cyber to learn how they operate and what need to be solved for them. And what we realized is that they basically had two main pain points. One, back in 2017, there wasn't like any technology for hot, or warm, or basically what I will define transactional wallets. DAVID LAWEE: Yeah, cold wallets was security. MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, there were like concept of cold wallets. And there were good companies like [INAUDIBLE],, and Coinbase, and [INAUDIBLE] that provided cold storage. And you can basically put those keys in some kind of bunker, where it's disconnected. But I will take you 42 hours to withdraw them and to make a transaction. And what we realized is that if the future of crypto, the future of digital asset, is really to replace the financial rails, then financial rails work in real time. Anyone who interacted with any form of fintech or financial offering knows that it works in real time. So it was great for us that this kind of cold storage technology might be really suitable for people who want to buy Bitcoin at $1,000 and then sell it like 60, after four years. But it's not useful for anything that is transactional. And there was no technology back then that was doing it reasonably well. And the second thing, which was actually less obvious, but was very clear to us, is that in crypto when you're doing a transaction between two parties, you basically have wallet addresses. And that's just basically a very long random string. And because it's an open public, private key system that is very variable and at the second that you send a transaction, basically the settlement finality or essentially the time that it takes the transaction to confirm and being not recursable is very quick. It's seconds or 15 minutes. Like 15 minutes is the slowest on Bitcoin. On most other blockchains today it's seconds or some it's milliseconds. So if you made a mistake of copy pasting a wallet address of your counterparty or you've been attacked by some kind of phishing attack, man in the middle attack-- and those were actually the most common attacks-- then you will basically burn the wire. The amount of funds that you intended to send to the recipient will go to the wrong location. Either they will go to some address that doesn't exist. Or they will go to the hands of the hacker. Or there was also, because we're talking about institution, there is also a fear from insider fraud, that one of the employees will basically misappropriate and will pull the funds into his own wallet and take the next flight to a place where there is no extradition. So that was like the second big problem. And what we've developed is essentially a system that had both the transactional wallet technology that was suitable for doing transactions in near real time for people. And the second thing that we solved for them is that they didn't have to deal with the addresses. And they had something that eventually became the Fireblocks network, but basically a connectivity to all their venues and counterparties that they were dealing without them doing this kind of very bespoke and manual processes to mitigate that risk. DAVID LAWEE: Yeah, anybody who sent crypto to anybody else has gone through that terrifying moment where you push the button and you're like, OK, did it get there? You're afraid of losing all your money. MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, like the heart attack moment. DAVID LAWEE: Yeah, exactly. MICHAEL SHAULOV: You're like-- you're pressing refresh on the block explorer to see. DAVID LAWEE: Yeah, it's terrifying. And it is for even really seasoned professionals. That's what's so interesting about it. MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah. DAVID LAWEE: What is the difference, though, between what you give a customer, or a customer using Fireblocks technology, versus, let's say, a MetaMask account, which may be more listeners are kind of used to using? MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, so MetaMask is a great product. It's basically a retail wallet, right? And to be honest, it's also kind of generation one of retail wallets. So first of all, the topology around the wallet is very different. In the MetaMask case, clearly it's kind of browser extension that connects to your Chrome. And the private key, there is basically one private key. That private key either leaves in the local storage of your browser or if you're a more sophisticated user, you can basically buy those hardware devices, like Ledger Nano. And it will sit on that kind of USB key. But you have one private key that sits in a single location, which means that only one user basically governs that private key. And you don't have any policies. So basically, the transaction that you send you have one chance to click approve or not, it will go through. So there is kind of single authorization. And you don't have that kind of network. So you eventually need to copy paste addresses. Or you connect with it all kind of applications. But you don't have any verification of where you're actually going to send your transaction. So it's a fairly bare bone wallet experience that is really designed for consumers with, I would say, maybe maximum flexibility, but generally speaking with no security. On the other side, when you deal with institutions, you really need something else. When an institution-- let's maybe take an example. When an institution deals with a bank, has a bank account, they have their internal policies of who can approve what wires in what amounts and how many people need to approve it, which we call at Fireblocks our policy engine. But essentially a kind of workflow that is designed to make sure that you have all the checks and balances before a transaction is being remitted. And you can put in place, if it's kind of treasury operations, you can basically put all the different policies and the workflows that you need in order to do multi-user approval. If you're working with API, so our platform is also designed for API, which today accounts for most of the usage, then you can also put all kinds of policies around fraud detection, too fast to basically, velocity in terms of the amount of transactions that you can have, the total aggregated value of transaction that you can have, and essentially break breakpoints in which when it hits those limits per transaction, or per some kind of aggregation, it will basically will start to be passed through for manual reviewer by fraud analysts, and definitely that sort of institutional network, which doesn't exist with MetaMask. At the core, by the way, and it's a really big difference, is that in Fireblocks you don't have one private key. We actually use a technology that is called multi-party computation, or MPC, or threshold signatures. It's actually all different buzzwords or naming conventions for the same technology. But the idea over there is that using an advanced form of cryptography, you're able to distribute the private key across multiple endpoints and effectively sort of reduce the single point of failure and the single point of compromise that if one user is breached, or one user tries to defraud the system, the transaction will actually go through. DAVID LAWEE: OK, I got it. That makes sense to me. So tell me the range of customers you serve today. MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, today it's pretty broad. So we have about 1,400 clients. They really go from really small hedge funds and player, like two guys and a dog in a garage that are working on it, say a hedge fund or some kind of trading technology tool. Again, all the exchanges that we talked about, some of the names that I mentioned earlier, are those days are customers. A lot of the institutional market makers, over the counter desks, brokers, and so on, they use us. A lot of the fintech apps, so last the year or so, year and a half, was a really big focus on the fintech app, folks like Revolut, and Robinhood, other really big players that I think are household names that they think people use and know we sort of powering all or part of their backend. Banks, so banks were fairly active in the space for the last year or so, Bank of New York Mellon been a big part of ours. Cross River Bank and a few other folks that we're working on on different type of projects. And then pivoting slightly to other categories that we started to engage in the last, I would say, six, nine months. On the one side is payment service providers, an example checkout.com, that empowering and working with. And on the other side is really Web3 developers that are working on games. They are working on new social media engagements, seeing big retailers trying to figure out how to experiment with NFTs for royalties and other interesting things that they can do. That's actually maybe the most creative, puzzling, experimental space that we are currently engaged with. Almost every project you look into there, it's kind of interesting. Initially, you don't fully get it. And then you think more about it. And sometimes it start to make sense. DAVID LAWEE: This is kind of stunning. And what makes you such an interesting person to talk to in this space is you have this range of customers that you're talking to on a daily basis from kind of, let's say, traditional crypto to things that are hard to even understand. And you have to manage all of these different chains and the connection to them because that's the whole purpose of a wallet is to connect across chains. And you need to manage these boom and bust cycles within crypto. And obviously, we're going through one now, a bust cycle. And that as a corporate planning exercise just seems so challenging. What's been your secret? Because you've actually done a pretty good job. When I first met you, you were talking about almost exclusively the trading. Then we started talking a little bit about customers that were doing stablecoins. And now I feel like Web3 is becoming an increasing focus. How have you been able to do it? MICHAEL SHAULOV: Well, we try to do it through the OKRs. But that's definitely probably not the magic behind trying to pivot across all those segments. So I think that the real secret here is really to be engaged with the market and to spend, in my view, as much as possible as an executive team, the product executive team, with all those customers and try to learn and understand the trends. I think that there were a couple of really strategic decisions that I wouldn't actually say-- some of them we were just lucky to take those turns, for example, into DeFi that eventually sort of dragged us into Web3. I think that actually the payments was much more thoughtful and organic in terms of how we've approached it. So I wouldn't say that everything is so calculated and we were able to predict some of those things. We've been in the right place at the right time. And we were paying attention maybe more than others with the right technology. But honestly-- DAVID LAWEE: I find there's so many people who are in the right place at the right time. It's just not a satisfactory answer. I get it though. It's super hard. I do admire the way you-- your personal learning agenda and how much time you spend on it. I certainly get a chance to observe that. I think it is much harder as you get bigger to remain nimble. MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, so I mean, I think that it basically goes back to what I said earlier about this kind of concept of the four steps, four steps, the epiphany, and all this customer discovery. And honestly, I probably don't have the answer yet to how to do it in a huge scale. This is an exercise that we're doing right now. We actually did some kind of reorg to try to, I would say, scale it. But to deploy that discipline that we need to spend a lot of time with the clients, make sure that we understand the pain, make sure that we crystallize the pain, make sure that we actually segment the market in the proper and right way and learn it. And then we deploy the resources to specifically solve from a product and engineering standpoint that pain. I think this is critical. I hope that we'll be able to continue and scale it as the market evolves. There is a slightly different exercise that, again, sort of to be fair, the jury's still out how we will be able to deal with it is actually to be able to market across such a broad set of use cases. That I would argue is the second part of that problem. To be honest, Google actually does it in a very good way to be almost this everything to everyone that we want to eventually be able to do that. At the core, interestingly enough, from a technical standpoint and the technology itself, we've run a pretty intensive exercise a couple of weeks ago. And actually, I think that at the core in terms of what we need to develop, the commonalities between all those different use cases, that matrix is actually fairly easy to diagonalize and create something that's reasonably consistent, and clear, and clean in terms of what's the architecture and what people need. But then eventually to make sure that everybody is aware that we are able to deliver it and do it, it's a not a straightforward marketing exercise. But we are committed to do it. And I think that there is a lot of network effects between those different segments that we will be able to leverage to make sure we're doing it correctly. DAVID LAWEE: I want to push on that a bit more because honestly, I'm almost confounded with how well you do it. I think Google actually has a much easier time because most of our business is kind of one business and one set of customers. And we've always had kind of a simple kind of mindset around prioritizing the end user. So we've not had to think about all of these different kind of instances, like focus on advertisers. There are so many things you could focus on. And we've always just had a very clear sense for what we are focusing on, which has made a huge difference as the company has scaled because someone in a room can be like, oh, we focus on the end user. And it kind of silences all discussion. Whereas, in your company, you have someone who's focusing on-- well, I guess you've probably segmented it. But people need to move around. But just to kind of push on it a little, what do the Web3 companies need in terms of wallet infrastructure? Let me put it this way. If I'm a Web2 game company, what are my options for bringing my new game to market? And how am I going to connect my customers to that? MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, I mean, at the very least, they have two problems that they need to think or to solve. The first one, which is quite easy-- and this is kind of the common thing that we have across all of our clients-- is the treasury management, how they as a company are able to buy ETH, mint NFTs, distribute those NFTs, collect revenue, do all their treasury management in the broader sense. There are basically things that may be in a very rudimentary you might not-- well, it's in treasury management. But if you just expand it slightly, you'd say, OK, this is all some kind of operational function that their CFO, or ops, or-- DAVID LAWEE: And by Treasure. Management, this is like I have my own token, whatever, game 3 token. And I need to manage the ins and outs of that token? MICHAEL SHAULOV: The ins and outs. Usually you also have some kind of component of on-ramping and off-ramping. By on-ramping and off-ramping mean that my user might not have crypto and they need to buy ETH or they need to buy a stablecoin by kind traditional form of a credit card. And they need to buy it for them and deliver it to them. But this is also a kind of financial backend operations that they need to do. The second part of the problem, which I would say that problem is still in flux and I think this problem will be in flux for the considerable future. And I think we talked about it a bit in terms of how eventually probably someone like Google and Apple will play in this space is really, how do you connect to your end users? Right now, they pretty much have, I would say, three options. Option number one is the option that some of the people on this call are familiar. You tell your users, download the MetaMask. When you come to the game do connect with MetaMask, or connect with wallet, connect wherever and use your non-custodial wallet. That's the-- DAVID LAWEE: Play your game. Play our game. Good luck to you if you lose anything. If you've lost your keys, good luck to you. If somehow you get hacked, good luck to you. MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, honestly, like to be very honest, I actually think that losing your key is almost like the second degree issue over there. The first degree is just like a regular user or regular internet user doesn't know what MetaMask is. And setting up the MetaMask and then at some point it pops up this message like, hey, please remember those 24 words. And I think that the experience over there of why even you need to download some kind of extension, and what is a wallet, why do I need that wallet, it's not a trivial experience. Someone needs to be educated on what that means, and why it is important, what I'm going to store in that wallet, and how I can interact with that wallet, et cetera. By the way, it's still not the most polished experience even if you're using the newest versions. But then you reach the point of what happens if I lose the keys? To be honest, I'm not even sure how-- it's definitely like a second degree issue over there because unlike with a lot of the base crypto assets, let's say Bitcoin, if you lose your keys, that's it. You lost access to Bitcoin. At least with gaming, NFT, stablecoin you can potentially re-issue. So there might be some very complicated. But there might be even a recourse. I just think that the first part of the problem, which is get your own non-custodial wallet, just so much friction that when you build a game, you really need to-- and this is a lot of the discussion that we're having with some of the gaming studios, is that the way they segment the target audience for their game is crypto native or not crypto native. DAVID LAWEE: Right. Right. MICHAEL SHAULOV: That's probably like how Zynga classified their target audience when they came out with Farmville 12 years ago. They probably had a slightly more intuitive way of we are interested in people that are like to play these games. So that's the first option. The second option is what we will call a custodial option. You don't have a wallet. Basically, the user is not required to have any wallet. He just gets like a wallet from the game developer, or from someone like Fireblocks, or from some kind of licensed financial institution. Honestly, probably not a bad option given where we at right now. DAVID LAWEE: So that's what I have with Coinbase? MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yes, yes, that's the experience that you have with Coinbase. That's the experience that you have with Coinbase-- DAVID LAWEE: There's probably 100 million people in the world who have had that experience, or something in that neighborhood, and maybe 15 million people in the world who've had the MetaMask type experience. MICHAEL SHAULOV: MetaMask I think has something like last I heard 28 million users. Custodial wallets in exchanges is definitely north globally, north like 300 million. DAVID LAWEE: OK, so 300 million. So it's a much more common experience. MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, it's a much more common experience. That experience doesn't really involve anything complicated. You just need to KYC someone. That's the friction, by the way. DAVID LAWEE: And it just feels like a regular internet account. I just input my password. MICHAEL SHAULOV: The main challenge over there right now is on the regulatory side because if you want to really use a full blown custodial wallet, as we call it, so if you had to onboard with Coinbase, then you would basically need to do a full fledged KYC. And for some of those offerings, especially games, there is a question of why because again, this is a legal opinion. DAVID LAWEE: And by KYC, what is that involved? MICHAEL SHAULOV: KYC is know your customer. So I still like most of the people on this call have opened a bank account-- DAVID LAWEE: I got to give you [INAUDIBLE] information, including identification and stuff like that. MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, bring me all the information you have, including your Social Security number, driver's license photos. DAVID LAWEE: So that makes no sense for a game company. And what's the third option? MICHAEL SHAULOV: And the third option is something that is currently in the works by a few companies, including ourselves, that are currently looking into it is what we call sort of assisted self custody, that essentially you use MPC to break the key between the user and the providers. In this case, you can actually have multiple parties on the backend. And it's still basically the user is in control. You can reasonably well abstract the experience. And you can also build some kind of threshold in the case that the user loses his key, or his wallet, or his phone, or whatever he is using. You can reprovision his key because there is sufficient threshold on the backend that is not concentrated with one party. This is the more novel approach. This is I think what we have. Those are the three-- DAVID LAWEE: And that one doesn't require KYC because the user has a little bit more control? I mean, they're still accessing it in the same way, right? They're accessing it with a consumer type username, password? MICHAEL SHAULOV: Well, they will have part of the key basically sitting either in the browser or in their mobile device. So from a legal standpoint, the legal definition, the provider, whether the game developer, or us, or whoever is the other side of that equation, is not in control and is not basically blocking the user in the case that they want to leave the system and take their crypto with them. DAVID LAWEE: I see. But to the user, will it feel like there's just two types of-- even though there's this legal nuance-- MICHAEL SHAULOV: Yeah, for the user it will probably feel much more-- you can make it feel much more like the exchange option, like the Coinbase option, but without the KYC, without the friction of giving all that information. DAVID LAWEE: OK, so that's my favorite option. So now I'm a user. I've got kind of, let's say, we're going three or four years forward. I've got some portable experience, where I go to MetaMask. I log in to every game that I play that is targeting crypto native gamers. And I have 15 other accounts at games that I like to play-- I'm a gamer-- that are all using some hybrid custodial, semi-custodial option. It sounds confusing to me. I've got my money spread across 15 bank accounts. MICHAEL SHAULOV: Right. DAVID LAWEE: How is that a good end state? MICHAEL SHAULOV: It's not. So that's why I think that at the end of the day, this is I think that eventually someone will need to step in with kind of share the infrastructure for that on the endpoint, whether it's like within Chrome or within the mobile ecosystem. I mean, to be fair, it almost kind of trivial that Apple and Google will be in some ways embed some simple service in the mobile devices. I mean, one of the main reasons for that is also from a manufacturing standpoint. You control the trusted execution. So basically, the secure element in the mobile device that is the best way to protect the encryption keys, to encrypt the private keys. So in theory, that all make sense. In practice, we are on this call. We know that it's not currently the reality. And I don't know. Sometimes things don't happen exactly as you predict them. But definitely, someone will need to come with an operating system service package that aggregates the wallet software service for the different players. DAVID LAWEE: Yeah, part of what's driving this is regulation because you have these kind of genuine concerns around money laundering, and fraud.
